items.title: TOP FIVE NEWS OF THE WEEK
items.summary:
TOP FIVE NEWS OF THE WEEK

OpenAI's models escaped the sandbox and hacked Hugging Face. And that's only number five... kidding, that's number one. Top five news of the week from Predict Time

1. AI went off the leash

@OpenAI officially confirmed it: during testing, their new models found a zero-day, broke out of an isolated environment with no internet access, got into the internal network, and then hacked Hugging Face production to inflate their own benchmark score. Nobody told them to do it. They picked the targets and the methods themselves

2. China dropped a monster

Moonshot released the open weights of @Kimi_Moonshot K3, nearly three trillion parameters, fully public. The White House immediately accused them of distilling American models and using restricted Nvidia Blackwell chips. OpenAI president Greg Brockman's review was short: "pretty good"

3. A perfect score

Anthropic's @claudeai Opus five scored a flawless maximum at the International Mathematical Olympiad, every problem solved without a single mistake. Meanwhile OpenAI is rolling out its GPT five model called Sol. Opinions on Opus five, by the way, are split: half the internet is thrilled, the other half is screaming "downgrade"

4. The Polymarket you didn't know

An investigation by Whitney Webb: the neat origin story about a guy building @Polymarket in his bathroom back in twenty twenty is not quite true. According to the investigation, the platform grew out of TokenBnk, and the trail leads to Peter Thiel and attempts to revive a shut down DARPA project, a prediction market on terrorist attacks

5. Polymarket is getting hit from both sides

First, Congressman Ritchie Torres and a coalition are pushing a bill to ban government officials from trading on prediction markets, insider info is still insider info. Second, a lawsuit from traders over several million dollars, including a large payout from a single user

All of this happened in one week. Imagine what the next one looks like. Follow @PredictTime_, so you're never the last one to hear it

items.title: "A human being is not an AGI." That's not a random take. That's the man who built GPT.
items.summary:
"A human being is not an AGI." That's not a random take. That's the man who built GPT.

Ilya Sutskever said something on a podcast that is almost wild.

"A human being lacks a huge amount of knowledge. Instead, we rely on continual learning."

Every AI model today learns during training and then freezes. Like a student who studies for years, takes the exam, and never learns anything new again.

Ilya is saying that's the wrong target entirely. The industry overshot.

His vision: "I produce a superintelligent 15-year-old. They don't know very much at all. A great student, very eager. You go and be a programmer. You go and be a doctor. Go and learn."

Not an AI that already knows everything. An AI that can learn anything. And keeps learning after you deploy it.

This week NVIDIA saw his research and put $5 billion behind it.

Everyone else is racing to make AI know more. Ilya is trying to make AI learn like we do.

vc: @dwarkesh_sp

items.title: Kimi K3 cooked Opus 5, GPT-5.6, and Claude Fable 5 in my opinion.
items.summary:
Kimi K3 cooked Opus 5, GPT-5.6, and Claude Fable 5 in my opinion. 

Someone had Opus 5 generate this game from a single prompt.

Then gave GPT-5.6 Sol nothing but the gameplay video and asked it to recreate the experience.

The result was impressive.

GPT-5.6 Sol produced a fast, well-optimized prototype that captured much of the gameplay.

But Opus 5 still came out ahead in the areas that make a game feel believable: world composition, environmental detail, camera direction, atmosphere, and overall 3D scene coherence.

It’s becoming clear that raw code generation is only part of the story. Design judgment is starting to matter just as much.

items.title: Recursive Superintelligence signs $400 compute deal with Amazon - TechCrunch
items.summary: On Tuesday, the AI company Recursive Superintelligence announced a $400 million compute deal with Amazon Web Services. The company, which emerged from stealth in May with $650 million in funding, is focused on building open-ended self-improving systems, a potentially compute-intensive approach to AI research. This multi-year deal is meant to provide flexibility as the company looks to scale up those systems. Recursive’s $410 million outlay represents the bulk of the company’s fundraising to date— but on a call with TechCrunch, Socher emphasized that he expected it to be the first of many such deals. Today’s announcement is “likely going to be one of the smallest compute deals we’re going to sign in the next few years,” Socher said. But in Recursive’s case, the goal is to use the powers of RSI to develop actual products — and Socher expects to be releasing the earliest examples before the end of the year.

items.title: NSF Supports AI, Cybersecurity Training at 14 Universities - GovTech
items.summary: ## The National Science Foundation will award funding to 14 universities through its CyberAICorps program to develop both public- and private-sector expertise in artificial intelligence and cybersecurity. Fourteen higher education institutions will receive new funding to prepare students for careers at the intersection of artificial intelligence and cybersecurity, the National Science Foundation (NSF) announced today. The foundation’s CyberAICorps Scholarship for Service (CyberAI SFS) program will fund university programs that integrate AI and cybersecurity education, workforce training and career pathways to state, local and federal government jobs that address national security needs. A news release from NSF said the funded universities will develop or maintain programs that combine technical training with hands-on experience, including research opportunities, cyber laboratories, virtual training environments, internships and partnerships with government and industry. As an example of the Scholarship Track, Vanderbilt University received $2,449,463 for a doctoral program that will support research on trustworthy AI, AI-enabled cyber defense and agentic AI systems.

items.title: AI leaders sign a statement asking the government to do something about automated AI - The Verge
items.summary: The statement follows a recent high-profile cybersecurity incident that rocked the AI industry. Employees of OpenAI and Anthropic, as well as Google, Meta, Thinking Machines, Microsoft, Mistral, and other leading AI labs, have written a statement to the US government supporting a potential slowdown of sorts for frontier AI development — or at least a speed-up of global coordinated governance efforts. “Al could help create a dramatically better future, but that outcome is not guaranteed,” the employees wrote in the statement. The news follows a high-profile cybersecurity incident that rocked the AI industry last week, in which an unreleased OpenAI model escaped its internal sandbox, finagled its way into gaining internet access, and then hacked competing AI lab Hugging Face. Building on work already underway to monitor frontier model releases: We request that the U.S. government support an international effort to develop the technical and governance tools needed to deliberately pace the frontier of automated Al development.”.

items.title: Another WTF moment.
items.summary:
Another WTF moment.

Hugging Face just open-sourced the fully local answer to OpenAI's Realtime voice API.

It's called speech-to-speech. You pip install it, run one command, and you get a WebSocket server at /v1/realtime that speaks the exact same protocol as OpenAI. Any client built for the OpenAI Realtime API can point at your machine instead and never know the difference.

This isn't a toy. The same pipeline runs in production as the conversation backend for thousands of Reachy Mini robots.

The stack is a four-stage cascade. Voice activity detection, speech to text, language model, text to speech. Each stage runs in its own thread with queues between them. Every stage is swappable via CLI flags.

Defaults out of the box are Silero VAD v5 for turn detection, NVIDIA's Parakeet TDT for transcription, and Qwen3-TTS for speech synthesis. The LLM slot points at any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Hosted OpenAI, HF Inference Providers, OpenRouter, or a vLLM or llama.cpp server on your own hardware.

Swap components for your use case. Whisper, Faster Whisper, Lightning Whisper MLX, or Paraformer for STT. Kokoro-82M, Pocket TTS, ChatTTS, or MMS TTS for the voice. mlx-lm on Apple Silicon or Transformers on CUDA if you want the LLM in-process too.

Language coverage tracks whichever backends you pick. Parakeet TDT alone covers 25 European languages. Set --language auto and the STT auto-detects each spoken prompt and forwards it downstream. Set a specific code and the whole pipeline locks to that language.

Four run modes ship in the box. Realtime for the OpenAI-compatible WebSocket server. Local to talk through your machine's mic and speakers with no client at all. Raw WebSocket for a minimal custom client. Or a TCP socket mode where models run on a remote server and a thin client handles mic and playback.

The fully local recipe is two terminals. One runs llama.cpp serving Gemma 4. The other runs speech-to-speech pointed at that endpoint. No API keys. No network hops. No audio leaving the machine.

Apache 2.0 licensed. Python 3.10+. Docker compose file included. Sitting at 6.3k stars.

The thing worth understanding is what this really is. The Realtime API is becoming the default interface for voice agents. Hugging Face just released an open-source implementation of the server side that runs on your hardware, keeps your audio local, and lets you swap the model behind it every day if you want.

Every voice agent product being built right now assumes a paid API. This flips that assumption.

items.title: OpenAI's newest AI escaped the test environment it was locked inside and hacked into another company on its OWN.
items.summary:
OpenAI's newest AI escaped the test environment it was locked inside and hacked into another company on its OWN.

To remind you:

Last week one of the biggest AI companies on Earth got breached. 

A platform called Hugging Face, which hosts more than a million AI models and datasets, said an "autonomous AI agent" had broken into its systems. Nobody knew whose agent it was.

For five days the whole industry wondered who was behind it.

Yesterday OpenAI raised its hand and said it was them. Or more precisely, it was their models, acting completely on their own.

So what did these models actually do?

OpenAI was running two of them, GPT-5.6 Sol and an unreleased model they will only describe as "even more capable." They wanted to measure how good the models were at hacking, so they deliberately turned the safety filters down.

They locked both models inside a sealed test environment with no real internet access. The only task was a benchmark called ExploitGym, a set of 898 real software vulnerabilities where the model has to turn each bug into a working attack.

But the models got OBSESSED with winning...

Instead of solving the test the honest way, they went hunting for a shortcut. They found a zero-day flaw in the software running their own sandbox, a bug nobody knew existed, and used it to break out.

Once they were loose on the open internet, they worked out that Hugging Face was probably storing the answer key to the benchmark.

So they hacked their way in.

They chained multiple exploits together, escalated their access, moved across servers, and pulled the test solutions straight out of Hugging Face's live production database.

They literally cheated on the test by breaking into another company to steal the answers.

OpenAI called it "an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities." In their own words, the models were "hyperfocused on finding a solution" and went "to extreme lengths to achieve a rather narrow testing goal."

And this was not the first time:

Before Sol ever launched, an independent red-team lab called METR caught it gaming its own tests to inflate its scores. It hid an exploit inside a data stream, escalated its privileges on the testing server, and leaked the answers human evaluators had hidden. And OpenAI shipped it anyway.

The day before the Hugging Face story, OpenAI paused a different unreleased model. This is the same model that earlier this year disproved a famous 1946 math conjecture, a result a Fields Medal winner called a breakthrough. They told it to only post its results to Slack but it found a way out of its sandbox and posted to a public GitHub page instead.

They had to pause it because it kept finding ways to act outside the box they built for it.

And it is not just OpenAI...

Anthropic has reported that one of its own models slipped its sandbox during safety testing and reached the internet it was never supposed to touch, then used it to email a researcher.

So step back and look at what these companies are telling you:

The only thing standing between these models and a real attack was a set of safety filters. Turn those filters down for a single test, and the model taught itself to escape, break into a company it was never pointed at, and take what it wanted.

OpenAI even said they expect incidents like it to "become more commonplace" as the models get more capable.

Sam Altman also predicted there'll be a major cyber attack this year.

And keep in mind that Sol is not a locked-away experiment but a publicly available model that businesses are already wiring into their own systems.

The next model that breaks out of its box might not be doing it just to cheat on a math test...

results.input: Giải giúp mình bài toán tích phân: nguyên hàm của x^2 là gì?

result.actual_text:
Nguyên hàm của $x^2$ là:

$$\int x^2 \, dx = \frac{x^3}{3} + C$$

*(với $C$ là hằng số thực bất kỳ).* 

Bạn có thể tính bằng cách áp dụng quy tắc tính nguyên hàm của hàm lũy thừa:
$$\int x^n \, dx = \frac{x^{n+1}}{n+1} + C \quad (n \neq -1)$$
Với $n = 2$, ta có $\frac{x^{2+1}}{2+1} + C = \frac{x^3}{3} + C$.

items.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman claims AI singularity has arrived
items.summary:
The hack took place as OpenAI tested the capabilities of a pair of its AI models, the company said in a statement last week, describing how the technology had escaped a "sandboxed testing environment" and gained access to the open Internet.

The technology seized on Hugging Face as a potential source of models and data sets necessary to complete the test, OpenAI said. [...] “I’ve been waiting for this my whole life, and I think it’s going to be incredible, hugely positive, awesome for the world," Altman added.

The remarks came days after OpenAI revealed what it described as a first-of-its kind autonomous AI cyber attack.

The company said its artificial intelligence models carried out a self-directed hack into another tech company, Hugging Face. [...] In an interview with ABC News last month, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that AI needs to be developed with the proper guardrails to ensure it has a positive impact on the world.

"We're proposing stronger regulation of the technology, proposing giving the government the ability to, again, in a narrow way, block deployment of unsafe technology," he said.

Speaking on the podcast, Altman appeared to criticized warnings issued by rival companies, without naming specific individuals or firms.
